questions.def: "Little" refers to an uncountable noun (evidence) and implies scarcity.
questions.question: ___ evidence suggests a correlation, but further research is needed.

questions.def: "Few" is used with countable nouns (applicants) and means not many.
questions.question: ___ of the applicants possessed the required qualifications.

questions.def: "Number" is used with countable nouns like "errors".
questions.question: Only a small ___ of errors were found in the report.

questions.def: "Much" is used with uncountable nouns like "information."
questions.question: ___ of the information presented was relevant to the discussion.

questions.def: "Some" indicates a positive quantity of time available.
questions.question: I have ___ free time this week, so I can help you.

questions.def: "Amount" is used with uncountable nouns like "research".
questions.question: A considerable ___ of research has been conducted on this topic.

questions.def: "Several" is used with countable nouns and implies more than two.
questions.question: ___ of the delegates expressed concerns about the new policy.

questions.def: "No" directly negates the existence of students who failed.
questions.question: ___ student failed the exam.

questions.def: "Much" is for uncountable nouns; use "many" for people.
questions.question: Much people attended the conference yesterday.

questions.def: "Quantity" is a general term suitable for seats.
questions.question: Only a limited ___ of seats are available.

questions.def: "Enough" indicates a sufficient quantity of evidence.
questions.question: There isn't ___ evidence to support that claim.

questions.def: "A great deal" is used with uncountable nouns like "time".
questions.question: He devoted ___ of his time to the project.

questions.def: "Plenty" is often used with "of" to indicate abundance.
questions.question: There is ___ of opportunity for advancement in this company.

questions.def: "Some" indicates a portion of the books.
questions.question: ___ of the books on the shelf are first editions.

questions.def: "Quite a few" indicates a sizable number of volunteers.
questions.question: ___ of the students volunteered to help.

questions.def: "Sufficient" is a general adjective meaning enough.
questions.question: We have ___ resources to complete the project.

questions.def: "Considerable" effort indicates a large amount of effort.
questions.question: ___ effort was put into the presentation; it was outstanding.

questions.def: "A minority" implies a small proportion of people were late.
questions.question: ___ of the participants were late for the meeting.

questions.def: "Abundance" works well with "of" to show plenty.
questions.question: There's an ___ of caution regarding the new procedure.

questions.def: "Scant" means very little attention was given.
questions.question: ___ attention was paid to the details of the contract.

questions.def: "None" is the most appropriate determiner here.
questions.question: ___ of the candidates had prior experience in this field.

questions.def: Use "each" or omit "of" and say "Every employee".
questions.question: Every of the employees received a bonus.

questions.def: "Majority" refers to the greater part or number.
questions.question: The ___ of respondents agreed with the proposal.

questions.def: "Insufficient" research means not enough research has been done.
questions.question: ___ research has been done on the long-term effects.

questions.def: "Most" is used with uncountable nouns like "information."
questions.question: ___ of the information is confidential.

questions.def: Use 'A' before a singular, countable noun that is being introduced in general.
questions.question: ___ considerable debate surrounds the ethical implications of AI.

questions.def: 'Few' means almost none, suitable for countable nouns like 'students'.
questions.question: ___ students attended the optional workshop.

questions.def: 'A number' implies several, fitting the plural verb implied later.
questions.question: Only ___ of attendees completed the survey.

questions.def: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like 'evidence'.
questions.question: ___ evidence suggests a correlation between exercise and cognitive function.

questions.def: 'A great deal of' is used for uncountable nouns like 'time'.
questions.question: She dedicated ___ time to the project.
